Dragan Stojicic. 21 Q. What is that person's official duty title? 22 A. He is head of the department for police affairs. 23 Q. At this time who is the Chief of Police in Prijedor? 24 A. I do not know which police you have in mind. 25 Q. Let me ask you, for some time, at least, Simo Drljaca was the Chief of Police in Prijedor. Does he continue in that position? 27 A. No. 28 Q. When he was in that position, what was the scope of his authority? Was it for the entire opstina or only for the town of Prijedor? 3 A. The Prijedor opstina. 4 Q. Who has taken his place? Who is now the Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor? 6 A. I do not know. The post of deputy is being performed by Dusan Jankovic. 8 Q. The Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor, who does that person report to? 10 A. You must ask him that. 11 Q. You do not know what the official reporting is from the Chief of Police upward? 13 A. I know what my responsibility is, but I do not know as regards the Chief of Police. 15 Q. Your immediate superior, does that superior report to the Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor? 17 A. Most probably, yes. 18 Q. Can you tell us when it was that Simo Drljaca relinquished his job as Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor? 20 A. I do not know exactly. I do not know the date but it was this year. 22 Q. Can you tell us when Simo Drljaca first took over as Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor? 24 A. I do, it was on 29th April 1992. 25 Q. Did he hold that post continuously until very recently? 26 A. Mostly, more or less. 27 Q. What time periods did he not hold that post, if you know? 28 A. I do not know. 1 Q. In the spring of 1992, prior to the attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac and other Muslims villages, prior to those attacks, what was your position in the Prijedor police department? 4 A. I was before the war deputy Commander of the traffic police, and the Commander was Fikret Kadiric until 29th April 1992. After that, I became the Commander of the traffic police station. 7 Q. What was Fikret Kadiric's ethnic group, if you know? 8 A. I do know. He was Muslim. 9 Q. On 29th April 1992 and 30th April 1992, the Serbs took over the positions of authority in opstina Prijedor, did they not? 11 A. Yes, that is so. 12 Q. When did you first learn that the Serbs were going to take that action? 14 A. On the eve of the 29th. 15 Q. So prior to that you had no idea at all that this was going to happen? 17 A. No, I did not know. 18 Q. How did you learn of that on the night of 29th April? 19 A. I was called in. 20 Q. Who called you in? 21 A. I was called in by my colleagues. 22 Q. Which colleague was it who you called you in? 23 A. My colleagues at work. 24 Q. Tell us their names, please. 25 A. There were quite a number of them. 26 Q. That is fine. Tell us the ones you remember. 27 A. All my colleagues who were working in the station with me. 28 Q. Tell us the names of those you remember, please. 1 A. I cannot remember any one of them just now. 2 Q. You cannot remember any of them? 3 A. No. 4 Q. Not even one? 5 A. Not one. 6 Q. These were colleagues you worked with daily? 7 A. Yes. 8 Q. You had worked with these colleagues for years? 9 A. Yes. 10 Q. Until you were called in on the evening of 29th April you did not know that this Serb takeover was planned? 12 A. I did not know because I never thought about it until the moment when at a common meeting we learned that the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was preparing to block barracks because we had been together with the other workers who were Muslim. 17 Q. Who told you that that was going to happen? 18 A. An official telegram arrived at the meeting and present was also the former head of department of the public security station, Hasan, the Commander, Fikret Kadiric, and representatives of parties, Mirzo Mujadzic and Simo Miskovic. 22 Q. Who else was present at this meeting? 23 A. For the moment I can just remember them and, of course, the other workers employed in the public security station. 25 Q. So you cannot remember your other colleagues who were present at this meeting? 27 A. Most of them were there, both Muslims and Serbs. 28 Q. But you cannot remember the names of any of them? 1 A. No, I cannot. 2 Q. Is it not true, however, that a secret Serb police force had been created months before this event? 4 A. I am not aware of it. 5 Q. Is it not true that it was this secretly created Serb police force that was ready and took over on 29th and 30th April in opstina Prijedor? 8 A. Your question is not clear to me. 9 Q. Is it not true that it was this secret Serb police force that was ready and in place and took over power on 29th and 30th April 1992? 12 A. I told you that I did not know that there was any secret police force until the eve of 29th. 14 Q. Prior to this takeover on 29th and 30th April 1992, you had frequent meetings with members of the JNA that were in Prijedor, did you not? 17 A. I did not. 18 Q. You did not meet with them frequently in your office at the police station? 20 A. No. 21 Q. Do you know a man by the name -- I am sorry, sir. Please go ahead. 23 A. Except for contacts that we had at a joint checkpoint which existed in Kozarac long before the war formed upon orders of the former Ministry of Internal Affairs headed by the Minister, Alija Deljimustovic(?). At that checkpoint, members of the military police were working. Those were the only contacts between the civil and military police that I was aware of. 1 Q. When was that joint checkpoint created in Kozarac? 2 A. Long before the actual events. After the events in the Republic of Croatia. 4 Q. Can you tell us what month and year it was created? 5 A. I cannot remember exactly, but before the war there was this checkpoint in Kozarac while Fikret Kadiric was still the Commander. 8 Q. How long did that joint checkpoint continue to exist in Kozarac? 9 A. It existed until the events that took place in Kozarac. 10 Q. When was that? 11 A. It was in May. I do not recollect exactly the date, but it was in May 1992. 13 Q. When you say "until the events that took place in Kozarac", do you mean until the attack on Kozarac? 15 A. I do not know what attack you are referring to. 16 Q. You are not aware of any attack that occurred on Kozarac in May of 1992? 18 A. Yes, but this came after events when a soldier was killed at Jakupovici on the road to Banja Luka. 20 Q. So when you say that this joint checkpoint existed until the events that took place in Kozarac, you are talking about the attack on Kozarac, is that correct? 23 A. No. 24 Q. What events are you talking about then? 25 A. The events after the killing of a soldier on the road that I mentioned. 27 Q. What events? What do you mean by "events"? 28 A. When the soldier was killed by Muslim extremists. 1 Q. What action did the Serbs take after a soldier was killed? What did they do in Kozarac? 3 A. I do not know. 4 Q. You do not know? 5 A. I was not au courant. I was responsible for the activities under my responsibility and not for military affairs. 7 Q. There were no civilian police at the joint checkpoint at Kozarac? 9 A. Yes, there were police from the traffic police station and the military police ---- 11 Q. So those police from the traffic ---- 12 A. --- they were. 13 Q. Those police from the traffic police station would have fallen under your jurisdiction, would they not? 15 A. My jurisdiction and of Fikret Kadiric who was working at the time. I was his deputy at the time. 17 Q. Did you know a man by the name of Zoran Karlica? 18 A. No. 19 Q. So, Zoran Karlica never visited your office in the spring of 1992 in Prijedor? 21 A. No. 22 Q. I believe you indicated that after the Serb takeover of Prijedor you became the Commander of the traffic police, is that correct? 24 A. Yes, that is correct. 25 Q. Who promoted you to that position? 26 A. The chief of the station. 27 Q. Who was that? 28 A. Simo Drljaca. 1 Q. Did he personally tell you ---- 2 A. I just took over. 3 Q. Did he personally tell you that ---- 4 A. I just took over ---- 5 Q. Did he personally tell you that you had been promoted to the Commander of the traffic police? 7 A. Not personally. I gave the documents later. I just continued the duties I had performed as a deputy and I took over as Commander until I was appointed when by a decision of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Srpska I was appointed to this post, but I was acting Commander until then. 12 Q. Who told you that you were acting Commander? 13 A. Simo Drljaca. 14 Q. When did he tell you that? 15 A. After the takeover of authority. 16 Q. That would be the next day after the takeover? 17 A. It was implied. I just continued the work I had been doing before. 19 Q. This would have been the next day after the takeover that Simo Drljaca told you you were the acting Commander, is that correct? 21 A. One may put it that way. 22 Q. How long did you hold that position? I think we may have lost it. Witness, I will repeat the question that I had asked. How long did you hold the position of Commander of traffic police? 27 A. Until 1994. 28 Q. Where was your office located, in what building, in Prijedor? 1 A. The headquarters of the station. 2 Q. Is that a building sometimes people refer to as the SUP building? 4 A. Yes, that is right. 5 Q. Have you ever been interviewed by any journalist, either Serb journalist or non-Serb journalist? 7 A. No ---- 8 Q. Have you ever given any ---- 9 A. --- not as far as I can remember. 10 Q. Have you ever given any statements for any newspaper, magazine, television programme or radio programme? 12 A. You mean the overall preceding period? 13 Q. Yes. 14 THE INTERPRETER: The interpreter cannot hear him. 15 MISS HOLLIS: I am sorry. We could not hear that answer. Would you repeat the answer, please? 17 A. There were professional statements in the domain of traffic exclusively local radio and television. 19 Q. Did you make these statements before the conflict or after the conflict? 21 A. Before the conflict. 22 Q. Have you watched any of this trial on television? 23 A. Well, every now and then because time permitting really. 24 Q. Which witnesses have you watched testify? 25 A. Not a single one. 26 Q. When you watched ---- 27 A. I watched -- I did watch the witnesses of the Prosecution, yes. 28 Q. Do you remember the names of any of those witnesses whose testimony you watched on television? 2 A. I think I only remember a Mirsad Mujadzic. 3 Q. How often did you watch these proceedings on television? 4 A. Seldom, seldom, because I worked, so I could not follow it all the time. 6 Q. Where would you be when you would watch this trial on television? Would you be at home? Would you be at the police station? Where would you be? 9 A. At home, at home when I get back home for work. 10 Q. Has anyone ever told you not to watch this trial on television? 11 A. Yes, I was told not to watch it when I found out that I would be a witness. 13 Q. Sir, when was that? When were you told? 14 A. I cannot remember the date exactly. I remember when Mr. Kay was here, then I was told about that. 16 Q. Do you remember what month that was? 17 A. Two or three months ago. 18 Q. In the spring and summer of 1992, what type of vehicles did the police use in opstina Prijedor? 20 A. They used vehicles with police plates and also civilian cars depending on the actual duty involved. We, in the traffic police, would use civilian vehicles when we were checking on speed limits, for example. 24 Q. These civilian vehicles, would they have any particular types of markings to identify them as police vehicles? 26 A. They were marked like any other police vehicle, that is, alarms and it also said "Police". It was written "Police". 28 Q. What colour were these civilian vehicles? 1 A. Civilian vehicles, it depends, red, white, grey. 2 Q. The regular police vehicles, what colour were they? 3 A. Blue and white, blue and -- there was white colour on the back and on the front, up front. 5 Q. What type of vehicles were they, what manufacture of vehicle? 6 A. In the traffic police it was primarily Golfs, a few Jugos, Zastava 101 and the like. 8 Q. Before the attacks began on Muslims villages in May 1992, prior to that time, how many traffic police officers were there in opstina Prijedor? 11 A. Together with the Muslims there were about 30 all together. 12 Q. And after ---- 13 A. Together with the leadership, I mean. 14 Q. So there would have been 30 total personnel in the traffic section of the opstina Prijedor police? 16 A. No, this is just the active personnel. The reserve personnel was much larger because it included Muslims too. 18 Q. How many of these reserve personnel were performing duties with the traffic police prior to 22nd May 1992? 20 A. Until after the takeover, there were reserve policemen who included Muslims but then after the takeover the Muslims left. 22 Q. Before the takeover, how many reserve police total would there have been who were actually performing duty, that is, including both Serbs and non-Serbs? 25 A. There were about 20 odd people altogether. 26 Q. After the Serb takeover at the end of April 1992, how many Muslims continued to work in your section of the Prijedor police? 1 A. None of them remained. They all withdrew to Kozarac and Ljubija. They joined their own stations there and they worked there. There were certain attempts to persuade some of them to work there, but they did not agree to that because they would have to sign a solemn declaration. 6 Q. What is this solemn declaration they would have to sign? 7 A. That they accept the laws of Republika Srpska and that they would enforce them. It is the usual kind of declaration that is made in police, like in any other police force. 10 Q. Did you sign such a declaration after the Serb takeover of Prijedor? 12 A. Yes. 13 Q. Did all of the police officers who worked for you sign such a declaration? 15 A. Yes. 16 Q. Did all the Reserve Police officers who worked for you, who came to work for you in June, July and August 1992 also sign such a declaration? 19 A. Yes. 20 Q. During the months of June, July and August 1992 how many traffic policemen worked for you in opstina Prijedor? 22 A. I cannot remember the exact number now, but depending on the actual needs we drew on the reserve force of the police. 24 Q. Well, what would be an average ---- 25 A. The number would change. 26 Q. What would be the lowest number that would have worked for you during that period? 28 A. I cannot remember specifically what the number was, but the number varied practically every day depending on the actual needs involved, and then we would draw on the reserve force because after the departure of the Muslims from the station it was normal that this had to be filled up. 5 Q. Was it filled up to the same number you had before? Were there more people working for you? Give us a general number, if you can? 8 A. Well, that number, about 50. 9 Q. This would include both active duty and reserve or just reserve? 10 A. The total number active duty and reserve. 11 Q. Can you ---- 12 A. Because ---- 13 Q. Please go ahead and finish. 14 A. Reserve Police officers had the same authority as regular police officers after they were mobilized. 16 Q. Where were you assigning these police officers, in what locations? 18 A. It was mainly checkpoints. 19 Q. Where were these checkpoints located? 20 A. Checkpoint Orlovci, Sana Raskovac, Sena Dolijna (?), etc., sometimes Gomjenica. 22 Q. Is the village of -- Mr. Prpos, can you hear me? 23 A. I can hear you. 24 Q. Is the village of Petrov Gaj located within opstina Prijedor? 25 A. Yes. 26 Q. Did you have any traffic police who came from Petrov Gaj? 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It looks like the picture is not working, Mr. Prpos is in the same pose. 1 THE WITNESS: No. 2 MISS HOLLIS: Your Honour, do you wish to stop -- no, we have lost it. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: How much longer do you think you have for cross and redirect? 6 MISS HOLLIS: Your Honour, I would think another 30 to 45 minutes perhaps. Your Honour, there is one thing I would ask, if we can get the picture back up, I am going to ask you to direct to this witness to provide the unredacted versions of the Defence Exhibit that have been discussed here today. So, if we could deal with that before we close this session. 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. Well, it appears that they are not getting the sound anyway or the picture. If it looks like they are getting it I will ask the witness to take his earphones off. What is the request? He has already done it. I will ask him again. Mr. Prpos, would you please take your earphones off? Thank you. Yes, go ahead, Miss Hollis. 19 MISS HOLLIS: Thank you, your Honour. During the course of direct examination the Defence referred to several documents and asked this witness questions about them. All of those documents are redacted to a greater or lesser degree. I believe those are Defence Exhibits 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77. We would ask that you order this witness to produce the unredacted version of those Exhibits for use both in cross-examination with this witness and also for other possible cross-examination or rebuttal. Your Honour, I suggest that the reason that we would allowed these documents is, number one, they have been referred to by the Defence and under completeness we would ask to review the entire document. Secondly, the other names that appear on that document would be relevant to us both to test the accuracy and the completeness of these documents which this witness has told us are very complete. In addition to that, they would be relevant to determine what types of duties these other individuals were purportedly performing who are named on these documents. So we would ask that you order this witness to produce them. 11 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Marro, we have asked Mr. Prpos to take off his earphones and we want to assure there is no Serbo-Croatian translation going on. 14 MR. MARRO: No problem, your Honour. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: "No problem" means no, right? OK, thank you. Mr. Kay, what is your response now regarding the request for complete documents? 18 MR. KAY: This request is not without its problems. We have had to extract these documents from Prijedor Police Station in the form that we have been given. What concerns me is that this may be a request that causes great difficulty for this trial and for this particular witness. He has made himself available to the -- well, he had made himself available to the Defence and I see an empty chair -- in the circumstances in which we are able to get these people to co-operate to the limited degree we can. I believe this Court knows a great deal from the evidence it has heard about the power of certain people in this particular region. They are not in positions that are easy and requests 1 that are made that can put them into personal difficulty, 2 particularly if they cannot be fulfilled, may have consequences 3 for those witnesses. I am not using this in a form of aggression but almost 5 like a intimidatory tactic against these individuals. What 6 concerns me is that there can be consequences that can cause a 7 witness and, indeed, this trial to have great problems. About 8 that I can say no more. I think the Court appreciates we have 9 obtained these documents and we have been into the police 10 station to get them. We have done our best.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What I hear as far as why the names were 12 excised, listening to Mr. Prpos, was he said those were not 13 relevant. The question becomes, well, who made the decision as 14 to relevancy? That is the problem. When they are turned over 15 to you and a decision is made by a person in power that, "This 16 is all I am going to give you", then that raises a problem just 17 in terms of our ability even to compel this individual to turn 18 over more. Certainly I imagine in any system, or at least in 19 any common law system, in terms of the completeness of a 20 document that is something that is recognised. What that means 21 is that one side should not be able to choose what it wants from 22 a document and put the document in and then not let the other 23 side see the entire document. I think that is a pretty 24 universal concept that would be recognised. Is that not true, 25 my fellow Judges? So the notion of completeness is not foreign and the 27 rationale is simple. It is to be fair for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have not made the decision on relevance. We have not told them to edit these documents. We were unable to see them until they were provided to us in this form. We have not asked for incomplete records to be put in this form before the Court. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Let me confer with my fellow Judges and see if they agree with me on my notion of completeness. Then of course there is a problem with just the production, whether we have the power even to do that. But there are questions I had about some of these documents and some names that I would be interested in. So it is going to affect how I might even look at these documents. (The Judges conferred). 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: My fellow Judges agree with my view on the notion of completeness, that is that if you offer part of a document then the other party can compel the entire document to be offered. The reason is obvious whether we are in common law or civil law I think. We want to have the complete document. The real power is our ability to compel. Judge Vohrah has suggested that there is no harm in asking the witness, directing him even, to produce the entire document. If he tells me, "Well, the powers that be made the decision that we would only give this", there is not too much I can tell him, I think, in terms of the power that this Tribunal has, unlike a national system. 24 MR. KAY: Yes, the Defence have no difficulty with the request. It is just that I am making a point to the Court about this as I do not want it reflected upon the Defence. 27 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I understand. I hope that the witness is still there and I will ask that he return. Do you have anything else to add, Miss Hollis, at this point? 2 MISS HOLLIS: Your Honour, we understood they were given these in redacted form. That is why we ask you to make the request, the order of this witness. We would note, however, that we have been told that in fact at least one or more of the Defence team have seen the unredacted documents even though they could not copy them. But again that really is peripheral I think to the problem here. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. Have you seen the complete document? 10 MR. KAY: Yes, but I cannot say I have memorized it or anything like that. 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It is Serbo-Croat and English. 13 MR. KAY: I insisted on seeing it so I knew what was being put before my eyes. 15 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: The reasons that were given you for the redaction were? 17 MR. KAY: It is a need-to-know basis as far as I am concerned. 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Pardon me? 19 MR. KAY: I was being treated on a need-to-know basis. I was being given only what I was going to receive. 21 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: So did you ask for more and get only what you received? 23 MR. KAY: Yes, and I asked to make sure that I could see an authentic -- well, I will not give evidence, but I asked to see something so I knew where it came from. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I think it is appropriate since there was mention of the fact that a member of the Defence team had seen it. I do not think you are giving evidence out of sorts. Let us talk with Mr. Prpos. Mr. Marro, would you ask Mr. Prpos to put his earphones on, please. Mr. Prpos, this is Judge McDonald talking. Mr. Prpos, regarding certain Exhibits that you made reference to in your testimony, the Tribunal is requesting that you produce the complete copies of these Exhibits. The copies that we have been presented are only partial, in that certain names and other information is taken -- can you hear me still? Can you hear me? 9 THE WITNESS: I can hear you. I can hear you. I can hear you. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Certain information is taken out of these Exhibits. You referred to them when you said that information had been blanked out. The Tribunal is requesting that you produce these documents completely without the blanked out portions, and they are Exhibits 63 -- these are Defence Exhibits -- Defence Exhibit 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77. Those are the documents that you made reference to today during your testimony. Are you able to produce those documents in their complete form without the blanked out portions or with the blanked out portions not being blanked out? 20 THE WITNESS: As far as I am concerned, because at present I am not in the Traffic Security police station, so all of that would be addressed to the present Commander of that station. So I do not have the authority now to give anything from those records because I am not authorised in that station now. These records remain in the station regardless of who is the Commander. 26 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Who is the Commander again of the traffic police now? 28 THE WITNESS: At present it is Mile Jankovic. I have testified on the basis of what I know in relation to the documents that were made while I was Commander of the police station. 3 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Miss Hollis, is there anything else? Mr. Kay? Mile Jankovic I understand is the present Commander. 5 MISS HOLLIS: Yes, your Honour. 6 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: He is the person who would have custody of these records? 8 MISS HOLLIS: Yes, your Honour. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: I do not know how I could compel -- I was looking at the witness list and I do not see him as a witness for the Defence. 12 MR. KAY: He is not, your Honour. He declined. 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: So he is not a witness. What authority do I have to compel? 15 MISS HOLLIS: What actual authority you have to compel even with this witness I guess is a question, but I might suggest that you request of this witness to pass your request on to Mr. Jankovic and have a reply tomorrow. 19 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: OK. Mr. Prpos, would you ask Mr. Jankovic if he will produce these documents in their complete form, the ones I referred to by Defence Exhibit numbers, so that you may bring them with you when you return tomorrow to complete your testimony? 24 THE WITNESS: I can try, but I cannot guarantee because this is exclusively within his authority. But I believe that insight can be made in a different way in terms of authenticating these documents. I think the people who have been crossed out are not all that important. These are simply the names of other policemen who do not want to appear in this kind of case. There are numbers and it is obvious that this is an excerpt in which Dusko Tadic appears. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: This is a trial and both sides want access to the information. So, if you will pass on this request, please, to Mr. Jankovic, and the request is that he give to you the complete copies of those Exhibits that I referred to by number, that is Defence Exhibits 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77, so that you may bring them with you tomorrow. You indicate to him that that is a request that has been made by the Tribunal. Would you do that? 12 THE WITNESS: I shall tell him, but as far as the outcome is concerned I cannot be the judge of that. 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Thank you very much, Mr. Prpos. You are now excused until tomorrow at 10 a.m. and we will resume the testimony then. The Court is adjourned until 10 a.m. 17 THE WITNESS: Thank you. 18 (5.40 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day).
